Portland.metaTitle: Wildlife Removal in Portland, ME | Cumberland County Pros
Portland.metaDescription: Rats, bats, raccoons and squirrels in Portland, ME. Brick and wood-frame homes from Munjoy Hill to the Old Port, with same-day service — call our crew today.
Portland.housing_era: Portland's housing runs from brick Federal and Victorian homes on the peninsula, triple-deckers and wood-frame multifamily buildings in Deering and Libbytown, to post-war neighborhoods off-peninsula. Sea captain's houses, old chimneys and shared rooflines are everywhere on the peninsula.
Portland.geographic_features: Casco Bay (working harbor and ferry-served islands offshore), Back Cove (tidal cove ringed by peninsula neighborhoods), Fore River (river and harbor channel on the western edge), Presumpscot River estuary (river mouth at the northern edge of the city)
neighborhoods: Munjoy Hill (dense older housing above the Eastern Promenade)
Old Port and waterfront (brick commercial blocks and restaurants)
West End (large historic homes and brick apartment buildings)
Deering and North Deering (residential neighborhoods off-peninsula)
Libbytown and Stroudwater (older wood-frame housing near the Fore River)
Portland.wildlife_intro:
Portland is Maine's largest city and its busiest wildlife market for our crew, because a working port, dense older housing and Casco Bay all meet on one peninsula. Norway rats are the signature problem around the Old Port, the waterfront and restaurant blocks, and they follow food waste into nearby Munjoy Hill and West End homes. Bats roost in the old chimneys and attics of brick and wood-frame peninsula houses, raccoons work chimneys and dumpsters, gray squirrels are in every canopy street in Deering, and skunks den under porches from Libbytown to North Deering.

Winter in Portland is severe enough that attics and wall voids stay occupied from late fall through spring, and the first warm weeks bring raccoon litters in chimneys and skunks under steps. Summer adds seasonal pressure around the waterfront and ferry traffic. Most Portland jobs combine rat exclusion, roofline sealing and attic inspection in one visit, because in connected older buildings a single open gap can serve several species. Call us and we will walk the building with you and explain the plan plainly.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Portland?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: Why do rats keep coming back in Portland's Old Port and Munjoy Hill?
faqs.a: The port and restaurant blocks provide steady food, the older brick and wood-frame buildings provide harborage, and sewers and utility lines provide travel routes. Removal alone does not hold in that setting. Lasting results come from sealing the building, tightening dumpster and waste practices, and addressing the entry points we find during inspection, floor by floor where buildings are connected.

South Portland.metaTitle: South Portland, ME Wildlife Removal | Knightville to Willard Beach
South Portland.metaDescription: Raccoons, bats, skunks and squirrels in South Portland, ME. Capes and older homes in Knightville, Ferry Village and Thornton Heights — same-day service, call us.
South Portland.housing_era: South Portland is largely post-war Capes, ranches and colonials in neighborhoods like Thornton Heights and Cash Corner, with older village housing in Knightville and Ferry Village near the bridge and harbor. Many homes have original chimneys and older garage and shed stock.
South Portland.geographic_features: Casco Bay and Portland Harbor (harbor shoreline along the northern edge), Fore River (river channel between South Portland and Portland), Willard Beach and Bug Light area (beach and breakwater shoreline), Clarks Pond and Long Creek (inland pond and stream corridors)

South Portland.wildlife_intro:
South Portland's neighborhoods sit between Portland Harbor and quiet inland streets, and the wildlife mix reflects both. Raccoons and skunks are steady in Ferry Village and Willard Beach area yards, where porches, sheds and beach-area trash give them shelter and food. Bats turn up in older Knightville homes and in post-war Capes across Thornton Heights once soffits age, and gray squirrels follow the mature street trees into attics. Near the harbor and Mill Creek, Norway rats appear around commercial waste and older waterfront buildings, though far less heavily than across the bridge in Portland.

Seasonal homes and summer activity near Willard Beach change the pattern in spring, when cottages and rentals open and owners find droppings or a den that formed over winter. Year-round homes get the winter version of the same work: animals in attics during the coldest months, then young raccoons and skunks in spring. Our crew seals rooflines and foundations, screens porches, and handles harbor-adjacent rat problems with exclusion first, so the fix holds after the animals are out.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in South Portland?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. Call us for an inspection and we will explain the options and the cost in writing before any work starts, with no pressure to decide on the spot.

faqs.q: Are opossums common in South Portland?
faqs.a: Yes, this far south on the coast opossums are a regular sight, especially near wooded edges, compost and unsecured pet food. They are generally not aggressive, they rarely stay in one den for long, and they do not carry rabies the way skunks and raccoons can. Usually securing food and closing off the space under a deck or shed is enough to move one along.

Westbrook.housing_era: Westbrook grew up as a mill city and still has mill-era multifamily housing in Cumberland Mills, older wood-frame homes downtown, and post-war and newer subdivisions toward Pride's Corner and Highland Lake. Westbrook.wildlife_intro:
Westbrook's mill history and the Presumpscot River shape its wildlife calls. Norway rats show up around older commercial and mill-adjacent blocks and the river corridor, bats colony in the attics of mill-era multifamily homes in Cumberland Mills and downtown, and raccoons and gray squirrels work the older rooflines on the residential streets in between. Skunks den under porches across the post-war neighborhoods, and homes near Highland Lake and Mill Brook see the added edge activity that comes with water and woods close behind the house.

The work here is often building-wide: an older Westbrook multifamily property may need chimney caps, soffit repairs and foundation sealing in several places before rats or bats stop returning. Winter pushes animals deep into wall voids and attics, and spring inspections catch litters before they grow. We explain what we find in plain terms, seal the building as a whole, and handle rats, bats and raccoons as one connected problem rather than three separate visits.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Westbrook?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. A simple squirrel entry sealed early costs far less than a long-standing bat roost or raccoon damage in an attic. faqs.q: Can bats be excluded from a Westbrook home in the middle of summer?
faqs.a: It depends on whether pups are present and whether the building is occupied. Exclusion from unoccupied buildings is not done in June and July under Maine rules, and MDIFW guidance discourages exclusion when flightless young are in the roost. We can inspect in summer, identify entries, and schedule the one-way exclusion for the right window so the colony leaves safely and does not return.

Scarborough.housing_era: Scarborough mixes year-round subdivisions in Oak Hill and Dunstan with dense seasonal cottages and beach homes at Pine Point, Higgins Beach and Prouts Neck, many built as summer places and later winterized. Cottage construction means crawl spaces, low eaves and older venting.
Scarborough.geographic_features: Scarborough Marsh (large salt marsh along the southern coast), Pine Point and the Scarborough River mouth (beach and river inlet), Higgins Beach (surf beach and cottage colony), Prouts Neck (rocky peninsula with seasonal homes)

Scarborough.wildlife_intro:
Scarborough gives our crew two towns in one: the year-round neighborhoods of Oak Hill and Dunstan, and the beach colonies at Pine Point, Higgins Beach and Prouts Neck. In the beach areas, raccoons and skunks den under raised cottages, bats roost in quiet summer attics, and squirrels enter through eaves weathered by salt air. Inland, the pattern is suburban: raccoons in chimneys, squirrels in attics and skunks under decks, with Scarborough Marsh keeping foxes, raccoons and other wildlife moving along the edges of neighborhoods near the marsh.

Spring openings are a major part of the Scarborough workload, when seasonal owners return to find a raccoon family in a chimney or bat droppings in a bedroom. Fall sealing before cottages close is the work that prevents most of it. Because many beach homes sit empty in winter, we focus on durable screening and caps that hold through storms, and we time any bat work around Maine's summer protections so young bats are not trapped inside an empty house.

faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much sealing or cleanup the house needs, so we do not quote a firm price before looking. faqs.q: Our Higgins Beach cottage had a raccoon in the chimney — how do we prevent it returning?
faqs.a: Start with a proper chimney cap and an inspection of the crawl space and eaves, which are the other usual cottage entries. Raccoons return to a den site they remember, especially females in spring, so sealing has to happen as soon as the animals are out. We also recommend a fall check before closing the cottage so winter damage is caught early.

Brunswick.wildlife_intro:
Brunswick's big historic houses are beautiful and, from a bat's point of view, ideal: large attics, multiple chimneys and decades of small gaps along Federal Street and Maine Street rooflines. Our Brunswick work leans heavily on bat exclusion in historic homes, raccoon removal from chimneys, and gray squirrel work in the mature canopy streets near Bowdoin. Toward Mere Point and the southern shore, seasonal cottages and coastal homes add skunks under porches, raccoons in quiet attics and the spring-opening problems that come with houses left empty in winter.

The Androscoggin River corridor keeps wildlife moving along the northern edge of town, and wooded lots in Cooks Corner and the outskirts bring animals close to newer homes as well. Winter denning drives the attic calls, while summer is inspection and planning season for bat work that must be timed around young bats. We take care to seal historic homes in ways that respect the building, closing entries without changing how a Federal Street house looks from the street.

faqs.q: Why do Brunswick's historic homes get bats so often?
faqs.a: Large attics, multiple masonry chimneys, decorative trim with small gaps, and a century or more of settling create many bat-sized entries, and a roost that works is reused year after year. Exclusion solves it by letting bats leave through one-way devices and then sealing every gap, including the small ones. Historic homes usually need a more detailed sealing plan than newer construction.

Gorham.wildlife_intro:
Gorham's mix of village homes, farms and new subdivisions produces a broad spread of calls. Gray squirrels and raccoons are the daily work in the village and the subdivisions, bats turn up in older farmhouses and barns toward North Gorham and White Rock, and skunks den under porches and sheds everywhere lots meet field or woods. Groundhogs work gardens and field edges in Little Falls and West Gorham, and much spring lawn damage blamed on moles turns out to be voles under snow, with hairy-tailed moles active in the softer soils.

Newer Gorham subdivisions are not exempt: builders' vents and soffit gaps give squirrels a way in within a few winters, and animals displaced by new construction show up in the homes around it. Our crew handles Gorham as a whole-property job, inspecting attic, roofline and foundation, sealing entries, and advising on trash, feed and woodpile placement. In winter we are mostly indoors with attics and chimneys; in summer the work moves out to decks, sheds and gardens.

faqs.q: Do newer Gorham subdivisions really get squirrels in the attic?
faqs.a: Yes. The good news is that new homes usually have fewer hidden entries, so a prompt inspection and sealing job tends to solve the problem completely.

Year-round homes follow the colder pattern, with attic activity peaking in winter and young animals appearing in spring. Our crew is used to working on both kinds of property in the same day in Windham, and we tailor the sealing to whether a house will be checked weekly or left alone until May.

Falmouth.wildlife_intro:
Falmouth's large homes and mature trees produce steady bat, squirrel and raccoon work for our crew. In the Foreside, big rooflines and multiple chimneys on coastal homes give bats and raccoons many ways in, and gray squirrels travel the canopy straight onto roofs. West Falmouth's farms and horse properties add skunks in barns and under porches, groundhogs along pasture and garden edges, and raccoons around feed storage. Opossums are regulars this close to the coast, usually found under decks or in garages where pet food is kept.

The jobs in Falmouth often involve larger, more complex buildings, so inspections take longer and sealing plans cover more entry points than a typical cape. Winter attic activity is common because these homes offer warm, quiet space above heated rooms. In spring we check for raccoon litters in chimneys before any exclusion. We work carefully around finished attics and historic details, and we explain the full sealing plan up front so there are no surprises about scope.

faqs.q: A raccoon is getting into our West Falmouth barn feed — what helps most?
faqs.a: Secure feed in sealed metal containers first, since an open food source will draw raccoons back nightly even after removal. Then we inspect the barn for denning, remove animals that have settled in, and close the gaps they use. Raccoons are a rabies-vector species in Maine, so droppings and nesting in a barn should be handled with care and cleaned properly.
